concerns.text: US-2 mandates the system 'implement a local simulation... to generate these ratings' if the dataset lacks them. In psychology, 'simulating' human perception ratings (outcome variable) without actual human raters creates a tautological validation loop. If the 'simulation' uses an LLM or heuristic based on text features (emoji count, punctuation), the outcome is mechanically determined by the predictors, violating the independence required by the research question (human-perceived intensity). This renders the correlation analysis circular and scientifically invalid.

US-2 Acceptance Scenario 2 requires the 'distribution of scores must show variance... to reflect human perception differences' via simulation. A simulation cannot 'reflect' human perception differences without an external ground truth (actual human ratings) to calibrate against. Generating variance arbitrarily or via a deterministic function of the input text does not measure 'perceived intensity'; it measures the simulation's internal noise or logic, failing the 'Human-Perception Grounding' principle in the Constitution.

US-3 Acceptance Scenario 3 requires calculating 'Cohen's d' for the relationship between emoji count (continuous/integer) and intensity (1-7 Likert). Cohen's d is a measure of effect size for the difference between two group means (e.g., t-test). For a correlation/regression analysis between two continuous/ordinal variables, the appropriate effect size metric is the correlation coefficient (r) or the standardized regression coefficient (beta), not Cohen's d. Using Cohen's d here is a category error in statistical methodology.
